title: RBI Faces Up to $12.7 Billion Bill From Record FCNR Deposit Scheme, Economists Warn
excerpt: The central bank's decision to absorb hedging costs on $136 billion in foreign inflows could squeeze its dividend to the government over the next five years.
body:
• India's FCNR(B) scheme and related facilities attracted $136.38 billion in foreign inflows — far exceeding the RBI's $80 billion target — but the hedging costs could reach $12.7 billion over five years.
  • The RBI agreed to absorb currency-hedging costs of 3%-3.5% annually for banks, shielding them from exchange-rate risk on the dollar deposits.
  • Emkay Global estimates the total cost at 1.2 trillion rupees ($12.7 billion) over five years, though IDFC First Bank says net costs could be offset by investing proceeds in US Treasuries.
  • A potential reduction in the RBI's annual dividend to the government could make it harder for New Delhi to meet its budget targets.

India's record-breaking foreign currency deposit scheme may have stabilized the rupee, but the bill for that stability is coming due. Economists estimate the Reserve Bank of India could face costs of up to $12.7 billion over five years from its decision to shoulder the currency-hedging burden for banks that participated in the program.

The RBI launched the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR(B), concessional swap window in June 2026 to defend the rupee after it hit record lows. Under the arrangement, the central bank offered to absorb the full hedging cost — estimated at 3% to 3.5% annually — for banks raising three-to-five-year foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians.

Inflows Far Exceeded Expectations

The scheme drew $127 billion in FCNR(B) deposits alone, nearly five times the $26 billion raised when a similar program was deployed during the 2013 balance-of-payments crisis. Adding $9.15 billion from overseas foreign-currency debt and external commercial borrowings, total inflows reached $136.38 billion — well above the RBI's $80 billion estimate.

"The funds raised need to be deployed judiciously and productively to mitigate these first-order and second-order fiscal costs."

— Madhavi Arora, Economist, Emkay Global Financial Services

The sheer scale of the response created a secondary challenge: the RBI must now absorb the additional rupees entering the banking system when lenders exchange their dollars with the central bank, adding to the sterilization burden.

Diverging Cost Estimates

Madhavi Arora of Emkay Global Financial Services estimates the combined cost of the swap facility and liquidity absorption could reach 1.2 trillion rupees ($12.7 billion) over five years. The RBI has not publicly commented on the cost.

However, not all economists see the price tag as alarming. Gaura Sengupta, economist at IDFC First Bank, argues the net annual cost could be as low as 100 billion rupees — or even marginally positive for the RBI — if the dollar proceeds are invested in 10-year US Treasuries yielding about 4.7%, which could generate more in interest than the hedging costs.

The RBI itself does not view the cost as a major concern, according to a person familiar with the central bank's thinking. The final bill will depend partly on how the proceeds are deployed, and India's foreign-exchange reserves — currently around $730 billion — are expected to grow enough to cover repayments when the deposits mature.

Dividend Risk for the Government

One underappreciated risk is the potential impact on the RBI's dividend to the government. The central bank transferred a record 2.87 trillion rupees ($30.4 billion) to New Delhi in May 2026, up from 2.69 trillion rupees a year earlier. Any reduction in future dividends stemming from FCNR-related costs could complicate the government's fiscal arithmetic.

Former RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao has publicly questioned whether the scheme was worth the cost. "FCNR deposits are borrowed dollars that have to be eventually repaid," he told Bloomberg in August. "They do not build confidence. What we need is confidence-building flows through foreign direct and portfolio investment."

What's Next

With the FCNR(B) mobilization window now closed, the rupee's trajectory will depend on crude oil prices — Brent jumped 7% this week amid U.S.-Iran tensions — global dollar conditions, and the pace of RBI intervention. Economists at IDFC First Bank expect the rupee to trade around 96 per dollar by December 2026, while Emkay projects a range of 95.75 to 97.50 through September 2027.

For the NRI diaspora, the scheme offered attractive returns on dollar deposits with full repatriation rights. The question now is whether those returns were too generous — and whether Indian taxpayers will ultimately foot the bill through a smaller central bank dividend.
nri_angle: NRIs who deposited in the FCNR scheme benefited from attractive returns with full repatriation, but the RBI's hedging costs raise questions about the long-term fiscal trade-off.
author: Diaspora Desk
